Constructing new ample divisors out of old onesThanks: Preliminary Version.

Paul Biran Address: School of Mathematics
Tel-Aviv University
Ramat-Aviv Tel-Aviv 69978
Israel. Email: paul@math.tau.ac.il
Date: May 1997
Abstract.

We prove a gluing theorem which allows to construct an ample divisor on a rational surface from two given ample divisors on simpler surfaces. This theorem combined with the Cremona action on the ample cone gives rise to an algorithm for constructing new ample divisors. We then propose a conjecture relating continued fractions approximations and Seshadri-like constants of line bundles over rational surfaces. By applying our algorithm recursively we verify our conjecture in many cases and obtain new asymptotic estimates on these constants. Finally, we explain the intuition behind the gluing theorem in terms of symplectic geometry and propose generalizations.

1. Introduction

The main objective of this paper is to propose a method for constructing new ample divisors on rational surfaces by gluing two given ones.

Recall that a divisor DD on an algebraic variety XX is ample if the corresponding line bundle 𝒪X​(D){\cal{O}}_{X}(D) is ample, and is called nef (numerically effective) if there exists an ample divisor AA such that A+k​DA+kD is ample for every k>0k>0. We refer the reader to [Dem, Ha 1] for excellent expositions on various aspects of the theory of ample and nef line bundles.

Of fundamental importance is the determination of those classes in Pic​(X)\mbox{Pic}(X) which are ample. Although this problem has a very simple solution for smooth curves, already in dimension two the problem becomes much harder. It turns out the even for relatively simple surfaces, such as rational, the complete answer is not known. Several conjectures in this direction exist, however at the present time only estimates on the ample cone – the cone generated by the ample classes in Pic​(X)\mbox{Pic}(X) – are known. For example, let d,m>0d,m>0 and consider the divisor class

D=π∗​𝒪ℂ​P2​(d)−m​∑j=1NEjD=\pi^{*}{\cal{O}}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(d)-m\sum_{j=1}^{N}E_{j}

on the blow-up π:VN→ℂ​P2\pi:V_{N}\rightarrow{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} of ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} at N≥9N\geq 9 generic points. Nagata conjectured in [Nag] that DD is ample iff D⋅D>0D\cdot D>0, but was able to prove it only for N′​sN^{\prime}s which are squares. In [Xu 1] Xu proved that DD is ample provided that md<N−1N\frac{m}{d}<\frac{\sqrt{N-1}}{N}. By making a more detailed analysis of the case m=1m=1, Xu proved in [Xu 2] that when d≥3d\geq 3 the divisor class D=π∗​𝒪ℂ​P2​(d)−∑j=1NEjD=\pi^{*}{\cal{O}}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(d)-\sum_{j=1}^{N}E_{j} is ample iff D⋅D>0D\cdot D>0 (see also Küchle [Ku] for a generalization for arbitrary surfaces and [Ang] for an analogous result for ℂ​P3{\mathbb{C}}P^{3}).

Closely related is the problem of computing Seshadri constants of ample line bundles, which measure their local positivity. The Seshadri constant ℰ⁡(ℒ,p){\cal{E}}({\cal{L}},p) of the line bundle ℒ{\cal{L}} at the point p∈Xp\in X is defined to be the supremum of all those ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0 for which the ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-divisor class π∗​ℒ−ϵ​E\pi^{*}{\cal{L}}-\epsilon E is nef on the blow-up π:X~p→X\pi:{\widetilde{X}}_{p}\rightarrow X of XX at the point pp with exceptional divisor EE.

Seshadri constant has been studied much by Demailly ([Dem]), Ein, Küchle, Lazarsfeld ([E-L],[E-K-L],[Laz]), and Xu ([Xu 3]). A considerable part of these works is devoted to computations and estimates from below on the values of these constants.

The present paper is largely motivated by the problem of computing Seshadri constants and the determination of the ample cone of rational surfaces. Our main results provide an algorithmic method for constructing new ample divisors out of the knowledge of ample divisors on simpler rational surfaces. By applying the algorithm recursively we obtain in Section 4 new estimates on Seshadri-like constants and detect new ample divisors. We then propose in Section 5 a conjecture naturally arising from our method which relates continued fractions expansions of N\sqrt{N} with the ample cone of ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} blown-up at NN points. Finally we interpret in Section 7 our main results in the language of Symplectic Geometry and explain the intuition behind them.

Our main tool is Shustin’s version of the Viro method for gluing curves with singularities.

2. Main results

Our main results deal with simple rational surfaces SS, which by definition are blow-ups Θ:S→ℂ​P2\Theta:S\rightarrow{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} of ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} at nn distinct points p1,…,pn∈ℂ​P2p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\in{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}.11 1 Note that we regard ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} itself as a simple rational surface too (this corresponds to n=0n=0). We denote by EiS=Θ−1​(pi)i=1,…,nE^{S}_{i}=\Theta^{-1}(p_{i})\quad i=1,\ldots,n the standard exceptional divisors of the blow-up and write ΣS\Sigma^{S} for the union ∪i=1nESi\cup_{i=1}^{n}E^{S}_{i}. Finally, we write LSL^{S} for be a divisor on SS, obtained by pulling back via Θ\Theta a projective line in ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} which does not pass through any of the points p1,…,pnp_{1},\ldots,p_{n}.

A vector (d,α1,…,αk)∈ℤ+×ℤ≥0k(d;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k})\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}\times{\mathbb{Z}}^{k}_{\mbox{\tiny$\geq 0$}} is called ample (resp. nef) if there exists a simple rational surface VV, on which the divisor d​LV−∑j=1kαj​EjVdL^{V}-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}E^{V}_{j} is ample (resp. nef).

Our first result is the following gluing theorem:

Theorem 2.A.

Let (d,m1,…​mn,m)(d;m_{1},\ldots m_{n},m) be an ample (resp. nef) vector and (m,α1,…,αk)∈ℤ+k+1(m;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k})\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}^{k+1} a nef vector. Then v=(d,m1,…,mn,α1,…,αk)v=(d;m_{1},\ldots,m_{n},\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}) is ample (resp. nef). Moreover, vv can be realized by an ample (resp. nef) divisor on a very general rational surface.

By a very general choice of points q1,…,qrq_{1},\ldots,q_{r} in an algebraic variety XX we mean that (q1,…,qr)(q_{1},\ldots,q_{r}) is allowed to vary in a subset of the configuration space 𝒞r​(X)={(x1,…,xr)∈Xr∣xi≠xj}{\cal{C}}_{r}(X)=\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r})\in X^{r}\mid x_{i}\neq x_{j}\} whose complement is contained in a countable union of proper subvarieties of 𝒞r​(X){\cal{C}}_{r}(X). By a very general rational surface we mean one which is obtained by blowing-up points q1,…,qr∈ℂ​P2q_{1},\ldots,q_{r}\in{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} which may be chosen to be very general.

We shall actually prove a stronger result which allows us to keep the blown-up points corresponding to the first ample vector fixed, thus giving information also on ample divisors on non-generic rational surfaces. The precise statement is:

Theorem 2.B.

Let DD be a divisor on a simple rational surface SS. Suppose that there exists a point p∈S∖(ΣS∪S​u​p​p​D)p\in S\setminus(\Sigma^{S}\cup Supp\,D) and m>0m>0 such that πp∗​D−m​E\pi_{p}^{*}D-mE is ample on the blow-up πp:S~p→S\pi_{p}:{\widetilde{S}}_{p}\rightarrow S of SS at pp with exceptional divisor EE. Let (m,α1,…,αk)∈ℤ+k+1(m;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k})\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}^{k+1} be a nef vector. Then for a very general choice of points q1,…,qk∈S∖(ΣS∪S​u​p​p​D)q_{1},\ldots,q_{k}\in S\setminus(\Sigma^{S}\cup Supp\,D) the divisor

π∗​D−∑j=1kαj​Ej\pi^{*}D-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}E_{j}

is ample on the blow-up π:S~→S\pi:{\widetilde{S}}\rightarrow S of SS at q1,…,qkq_{1},\ldots,q_{k} with exceptional divisors Ej=π−1​(qj)E_{j}=\pi^{-1}(q_{j}).

Proofs of Theorems 2.A and 2.B appear in Section 3.

Theorem 2.A in combination with the action of the Cremona group on the ample cone give rise to an algorithmic procedure for detecting new ample classes in the Picard group of rational surfaces. The algorithm will be explained in Section 4.2.

2.1. Applications to Seshadri constants

Given an ample line bundle ℒ→S{\cal{L}}\rightarrow S on a surface, and a vector w=(w1,…,wN)w=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{N}) of positive numbers we define the ww-weighted remainder of ℒ{\cal{L}} at the NN distinct points p1,…,pN∈Sp_{1},\ldots,p_{N}\in S to be the quantity

ℛw(ℒ,p1,…,pN)=1ℒ⋅ℒinf0≤ϵ∈ℝ{ℒϵ⋅ℒϵ|ℒϵ=π∗ℒ−ϵ∑j=1NwjEjis nef},{\cal{R}}^{w}({\cal{L}},p_{1},\ldots,p_{N})=\frac{1}{{\cal{L}}\cdot{\cal{L}}}\inf_{0\leq\epsilon\in{\mathbb{R}}}\left\{{\cal{L}}_{\epsilon}\cdot{\cal{L}}_{\epsilon}\bigg|{\cal{L}}_{\epsilon}=\pi^{*}{\cal{L}}-\epsilon\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}E_{j}\quad\mbox{is nef}\right\},

where π:S~→S\pi:{\widetilde{S}}\rightarrow S is the blow-up of SS at the points p1,…,pNp_{1},\ldots,p_{N} with exceptional divisors Ei=π−1​(pi)E_{i}=\pi^{-1}(p_{i}). It is obvious that 0≤ℛw<10\leq{\cal{R}}^{w}<1. Note that ℛw{\cal{R}}^{w} remains invariant under rescalings of ℒ{\cal{L}} and of ww, namely ℛa​w​(b​ℒ,p1,…​pN)=ℛw​(ℒ,p1,…​pN){\cal{R}}^{aw}(b{\cal{L}},p_{1},\ldots p_{N})={\cal{R}}^{w}({\cal{L}},p_{1},\ldots p_{N}) for every a,b>0a,b>0. It is convenient to define also a more global invariant, namely

ℛNw(ℒ)=inf{ℛw(ℒ,p1,…pN)∣p1,…pN∈Sare distinct points}.{\cal{R}}^{w}_{N}({\cal{L}})=\inf\left\{{\cal{R}}^{w}({\cal{L}},p_{1},\ldots p_{N})\mid p_{1},\ldots p_{N}\in S\quad\mbox{are distinct points}\right\}.

Restricting to the case of homogeneous weights we obtain the homogeneous remainders

ℛ⁡(ℒ,p1,…,pN)=ℛwh​(ℒ,p1,…,pN),ℛN​(ℒ)=ℛwh​(ℒ),{\cal{R}}({\cal{L}},p_{1},\ldots,p_{N})={\cal{R}}^{w_{h}}({\cal{L}},p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}),\qquad{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal{L}})={\cal{R}}^{w_{h}}({\cal{L}}),

where wh=(1,…,1)w_{h}=(1,\ldots,1).

The constants ℛw​(ℒ,p1,…,pN){\cal{R}}^{w}({\cal{L}},p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}) are obvious generalizations of the Seshadri constants ℰ⁡(ℒ,p){\cal{E}}({\cal{L}},p) from section 1 (see also [Xu 3] for similar Seshadri-like constants). Several theorems and conjectures related to the ample cone can be neatly formulated using the constants ℛN{\cal{R}}_{N}. For example, Nagata’s conjecture from Section 1 can be reformulated as “ ℛN​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1))=0{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1))=0 when N≥9N\geq 9 ”. Similarly, Xu’s result from Section 1 asserts that ℛN​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1))≤1N{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1))\leq\frac{1}{N}. In Section 4.3 we shall prove the following asymptotic result:

Theorem 2.1.A.
  1. 1)

    For N=a2​l2+2​lN=a^{2}l^{2}+2l, a,l∈ℕa,l\in{\mathbb{N}} ℛN​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1))≤1(a2​l+1)2{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1))\leq\frac{1}{(a^{2}l+1)^{2}}.

  2. 2)

    For N=a2​l2−2​lN=a^{2}l^{2}-2l, a,l,∈ℕa,l,\in{\mathbb{N}} ℛN​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1))≤1(a2​l−1)2{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1))\leq\frac{1}{(a^{2}l-1)^{2}}.

Then ℛN​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1))≤1(2​a2​l+1)2{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1))\leq\frac{1}{(2a^{2}l+1)^{2}}.

In Section 5 we shall view this result in a more general context by proposing a conjecture which bounds ℛN​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1)){\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1)) in terms of continued fractions approximations of N\sqrt{N}.

Our methods also yield, as a corollary, the following generalization of a theorem of Xu [Xu 2] and Küchle [Ku]:

Corollary 2.1.B.

Let d>0d>0. The divisor D=π∗​𝒪ℂ​P2​(d)−2​∑j=1NEjD=\pi^{*}{\cal{O}}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(d)-2\sum_{j=1}^{N}E_{j} on the blow-up of ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} at NN very general points is nef iff D⋅D≥0D\cdot D\geq 0.

The proof appears in Section 4.3. Let us conclude this section with the following, somewhat amusing, corollary of Theorem 2.A.

Corollary 2.1.C.

If Nagata’s conjecture holds for N1N_{1} and N2N_{2} then it holds also for N1​N2N_{1}N_{2}.

The proof is given in Section 4.4.

3. Gluing curves on rational surfaces

We shall derive Theorem 2.A as a corollary from Theorem 2.B. The proof of Theorem 2.B is based on a technique for ”gluing” singular curves, which was developed by Shustin in [Sh 1]. This method generalizes Viro’s method (see [Vi]) for gluing curves to singular cases.

Suppose that C1,…,CnC_{1},\ldots,C_{n} are plane curves with Newton Polygons Δ1,…,Δn\Delta_{1},\ldots,\Delta_{n} which have mutually disjoint interiors and match together to a bigger polygon Δ=Δ1∪…∪Δn\Delta=\Delta_{1}\cup\ldots\cup\Delta_{n}. Shustin’s method allows, under some transversality conditions on the equisingular strarta corresponding to C1,…,CnC_{1},\ldots,C_{n}, to construct a new curve CC with Newton polygon Δ\Delta and with singular points ”inherited” from C1,…,CnC_{1},\ldots,C_{n}. We refer the reader to [Sh 1] for a detailed presentation of the general method and to [Sh 2] for interesting applications in other directions. Here, we shall make use only of a tip of the power of this method, by applying it to two curves with disjoint Newton polygons.

The application of Shustin’s technique to our problem is summed up in the following proposition which will be the main ingredient in the proof of Theorem 2.B. Most of the proof presented below is essentially an adjustment of the arguments appearing in the proof of Theorem 3.1 of [Sh 1] to our specific situation.

Proposition 3.A.

Let DD be an effective divisor on a simple rational surface SS, and p∈S∖ΣSp\in S\setminus\Sigma^{S} a point with multp​D=m>0\mbox{mult}_{p}D=m>0. Let CC be an effective divisor on another simple rational surface VV, lying in the linear system |m′​LV−∑j=1kαj​EjV||m^{\prime}L^{V}-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}E^{V}_{j}|. Suppose that D,CD,C satisfy the following conditions:

  1. 1)

    0<m′<m0<m^{\prime}<m.

  2. 2)

    H1​(S~p,𝒪S~p​(πp∗​D−m​E))=0H^{1}({\widetilde{S}}_{p},{\cal{O}}_{{\widetilde{S}}_{p}}(\pi^{*}_{p}D-mE))=0, where πp:S~p→S\pi_{p}:{\widetilde{S}}_{p}\rightarrow S is the blow-up of SS at the point pp with exceptional divisor EE.

  3. 3)

    H1​(V,𝒪V​(C))=0H^{1}(V,{\cal{O}}_{V}(C))=0.

  4. 4)

    Each of C,DC,D does not have any of the standard exceptional divisors EiV,EjSE^{V}_{i},E^{S}_{j} as one of its components.

  5. 5)

    DD is an irreducible curve.

Then, there exist kk distinct points q1,…​qk∈S∖(ΣS∪S​u​p​p​D)q_{1},\ldots q_{k}\in S\setminus(\Sigma^{S}\cup Supp\,D) and a curve D~\widetilde{D} on the blow-up π:S~→S\pi:{\widetilde{S}}\rightarrow S of SS at q1,…,qkq_{1},\ldots,q_{k} with exceptional divisors Ej=π−1​(qj)E_{j}=\pi^{-1}(q_{j}), which has the following properties:

  1. 1)

    D~∈|π∗​D−∑j=1kαj​Ej|\widetilde{D}\in|\pi^{*}D-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}E_{j}|.

  2. 2)

    The curve D~\widetilde{D} is irreducible.

Proof.

The idea of the proof is basically the following. By passing to the underlying projective planes of S~p{\widetilde{S}}_{p} and VV we obtain from DD and CC two singular curves C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} and a point, still denoted by pp, such that multp​C1>deg⁡C2\mbox{mult}_{p}C_{1}>\deg C_{2}. This inequality implies that the Newton polygons of C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} with respect to an affine chart centered at pp are disjoint. The next step is to construct two deformations C1,tC_{1,t} and C2,tC_{2,t} of C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} which are equisingular for t>0t>0 and such that each of them contains a deformations of the union of the singular points of C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} except of the one at the point pp which might disappear. These two deformations are then glued using the Viro polynomial. Shustin’s method requires the Newton polygons of each of C1,tC_{1,t} and C2,tC_{2,t} to be contained in the union, say Δ\Delta, of the ones of C1C_{1} and C2C_{2}. In order to construct deformations which satisfy this, one has to prove roughly speaking that the equisingular strata of C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} intersect transversally the space of curves with Newton polygons Δ\Delta. This is precisely what the conditions of vanishing of the H1H^{1}’s is needed for.

Let us give now the precise details of the proof. Suppose that SS is obtained by blowing-up ΘS:S→ℂ​P2\Theta_{S}:S\rightarrow{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} at p1,…,pN∈ℂ​P2p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}\in{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} and that VV is obtained by blowing-up ΘV:V→ℂ​P2\Theta_{V}:V\rightarrow{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} at q10,…,qk0∈ℂ​P2q_{1}^{0},\ldots,q_{k}^{0}\in{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}. Put p0=ΘS​(p),C1=ΘS​(D)⊂ℂ​P2p_{0}=\Theta_{S}(p),\quad C_{1}=\Theta_{S}(D)\subset{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} and C2=ΘV​(C)⊂ℂ​P2C_{2}=\Theta_{V}(C)\subset{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}. Assuming that D∈|d​LS−∑i=1nmi​EiS|D\in|dL^{S}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{i}E^{S}_{i}| we see that:

  • •

    C1C_{1} is a plane curve of degree dd and has singularities of orders m1,…,mnm_{1},\ldots,m_{n} at the points p1,…,pnp_{1},\ldots,p_{n} and a singular point of order mm at p0p_{0}.

  • •

    C2C_{2} is a plane curve of degree m′m^{\prime} and has singularities of orders α1,…,αk\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k} at the points q10,…,qk0q_{1}^{0},\ldots,q_{k}^{0}.

In view of what we have to prove there is no loss of generality in assuming that qj0∉C1q_{j}^{0}\not\in C_{1} for every 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k. Choose an affine chart ℂ2⊂ℂ​P2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\subset{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} with coordinates (x,y)(x,y) such that p0=(0,0)p_{0}=(0,0) and such that p1,…,pn,q10,…,qk0∈(ℂ∗)2⊂ℂ2⊂ℂ​P2p_{1},\ldots,p_{n},q_{1}^{0},\ldots,q_{k}^{0}\in({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{2}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\subset{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}.

Let F1​(x,y),F2​(x,y)F_{1}(x,y),F_{2}(x,y) be polynomials of degrees dd and m′m^{\prime} respectively, such that C1∩ℂ2={F1=0}C_{1}\cap{\mathbb{C}}^{2}=\{F_{1}=0\} and C2∩ℂ2={F2=0}C_{2}\cap{\mathbb{C}}^{2}=\{F_{2}=0\}. Set

Δ1={(i,j)∈ℤ≥02|m≤i+j≤d},Δ2={(i,j)∈ℤ≥02|0≤i+j≤m′},\Delta_{1}=\{(i,j)\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}_{\geq 0}|m\leq i+j\leq d\},\qquad\Delta_{2}=\{(i,j)\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}_{\geq 0}|0\leq i+j\leq m^{\prime}\},

and put Δ=Δ1∪Δ2\Delta=\Delta_{1}\cup\Delta_{2}. With these notations, we may write

F1​(x,y)=∑(i,j)∈Δ1ai​j​xi​yj,F2​(x,y)=∑(i,j)∈Δ2ai​j​xi​yj.F_{1}(x,y)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\Delta_{1}}a_{ij}x^{i}y^{j},\qquad F_{2}(x,y)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\Delta_{2}}a_{ij}x^{i}y^{j}.

Let Δ¯1⊃Δ1\overline{\Delta}_{1}\supset\Delta_{1} and Δ¯2⊃Δ2\overline{\Delta}_{2}\supset\Delta_{2} be two slightly larger triangles with disjoint interiors. More precisely, let δ>0\delta>0 be a small enough number such that m′+2​δ<d−2​δm^{\prime}+2\delta<d-2\delta and set

Δ¯1={(i,j)∈ℝ≥02|m−δ≤i+j≤d},Δ¯1={(i,j)∈ℝ≥02|0≤i+j≤m′+δ}.\overline{\Delta}_{1}=\{(i,j)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}_{\geq 0}|m-\delta\leq i+j\leq d\},\qquad\overline{\Delta}_{1}=\{(i,j)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}_{\geq 0}|0\leq i+j\leq m^{\prime}+\delta\}.

Next, choose a strictly convex continuous piecewise linear function ν:ℝ2→ℝ\nu:{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}} such that the restrictions of ν\nu to each of Δ¯1,Δ¯2\overline{\Delta}_{1},\overline{\Delta}_{2} coincides with some linear function ℓ1,ℓ2:ℝ2→ℝ\ell_{1},\ell_{2}:{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}} with ℓ1≠ℓ2\ell_{1}\neq\ell_{2}. We shall define the curve D~\widetilde{D} as the zero locus of a polynomial lying in the following family:

Ft​(x,y)=∑(i,j)∈ΔAi​j​(t)​xi​yj​tν⁡(i,j)t>0,F_{t}(x,y)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\Delta}A_{ij}(t)x^{i}y^{j}t^{\nu(i,j)}\qquad t>0,

with limt→0Ai​j​(t)=ai​j\lim_{t\to 0}A_{ij}(t)=a_{ij}. The polynomial FtF_{t} is called the Viro polynomial.

More precisely, we claim that by a correct choice of of the coefficients Ai​j​(t)A_{ij}(t), and of a homogeneous change of coordinates (x,y)→Tt​(x,y)(x,y)\rightarrow T_{t}(x,y), the curve Dt={Ft(Tt(x,y))=0}D_{t}=\{F_{t}(T_{t}(x,y))=0\} will have the following properties for t>0t>0 small enough:

  1. 1)

    multpi​Dt=mi\mbox{mult}_{p_{i}}D_{t}=m_{i} for every 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

  2. 2)

    There exists kk points q1t,…,qkt{q_{1}}_{t},\ldots,{q_{k}}_{t} depending smoothly on t>0t>0 such that qjt≠pi{q_{j}}_{t}\neq p_{i} for every i,ji,j and multqjt​Dt=αj\mbox{mult}_{{q_{j}}_{t}}D_{t}=\alpha_{j} for every 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k.

  3. 3)

3.1. Passing from specific points to very general

In what follows we shall detect several useful ample (resp. nef) vectors (d,α1,…,αk)(d;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}) by choosing kk points q1,…,qk∈ℂ​P2q_{1},\ldots,q_{k}\in{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} to lie in a very specific convenient position which is not generic. The following lemma shows that this vectors remain ample (resp. nef) also for a very general choice of the points q1,…,qkq_{1},\ldots,q_{k}.

Lemma 3.1.A.

Let FF be a divisor on a simple rational surface SS, and q1(0),…​qk(0)∈S∖(ΣS∪S​u​p​p​F)q^{(0)}_{1},\ldots q^{(0)}_{k}\in S\setminus(\Sigma^{S}\cup Supp\,F) distinct points. π∗​F−∑j=1kfj​Ej\pi^{*}F-\sum_{j=1}^{k}f_{j}E_{j}

The idea of the proof is very simple. Since F~0=π0∗​F−∑j=1kfj​Ej0\widetilde{F}_{0}=\pi^{*}_{0}F-\sum_{j=1}^{k}f_{j}E^{0}_{j} is assumed to be nef on the blow-up of SS at q10,…​qk0q^{0}_{1},\ldots q^{0}_{k}, all the divisor classes which intersect F~0\widetilde{F}_{0} negatively do not admit any effective representatives. Now, the point is that if a divisor class on the blow-up of SS at specific points has no effective representatives then the same will continue to hold also on the blow-up at generic points. The lemma now follows because Pic​(S~)\mbox{Pic}({\widetilde{S}}) is countable. Let us give now the precise details.

We prove the lemma for the “nef” case, the “ample” being very similar. Consider the following subset of Pic​(S)×ℤ≥0k\mbox{Pic}(S)\times{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^{k}:

Obviously 𝒱{\cal{V}} is a very general subset of 𝒞k​(S∖(ΣS∪S​u​p​p​F)){\cal{C}}_{k}(S\setminus(\Sigma^{S}\cup Supp\,F)) having the needed properties.

Let us prove the existence of the Zariski-open sets 𝒰B{\cal{U}}_{B} claimed above. For this end put 𝒞=𝒞k​(S∖(ΣS∪S​u​p​p​F)),X=𝒞×S{\cal{C}}={\cal{C}}_{k}(S\setminus(\Sigma^{S}\cup Supp\,F)),\quad X={\cal{C}}\times S, and denote by p​r:X→𝒞pr:X\rightarrow{\cal{C}} the obvious projection.

3.2. Proof of the gluing Theorem

Now we are in position to prove Theorem 2.B.

4. Asymptotics on the remainders of 𝒪ℂ​P2​(1){\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1)

In order to obtain estimates on ℛN​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1)){\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1)) we shall extensively use Theorem 2.A in combination with the Cremona action. The point is, that the Cremona group acts on the set of ample (resp. nef) vectors. Let us briefly summerize the needed facts about the Cremona action. We refer the reader to [Do-Or] for more details.

4.1. The Cremona action on the ample cone

Denote by (Hk,⟨,⟩)(k≥3)(H_{k},\langle\,,\,\rangle)\quad(k\geq 3) the hyperbolic lattice Hk=ℤ​l⊕ℤ​e1⊕…⊕ℤ​ekH_{k}={\mathbb{Z}}l\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}e_{1}\oplus\ldots\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}e_{k} with the bilinear form ⟨,⟩\langle\,,\,\rangle defined by ⟨l,l⟩=1,⟨l,ej⟩=0,⟨ei,ej⟩=−δi​j\langle l,l\rangle=1,\quad\langle l,e_{j}\rangle=0,\quad\langle e_{i},e_{j}\rangle=-\delta_{ij}. Consider the subgroup Crk⊂Aut(Hk,⟨,⟩)Cr_{k}\subset Aut(H_{k},\langle\,,\,\rangle), generated by:

  1. 1)

    The symmetric group Sk↪Aut(Hk,⟨,⟩)S_{k}\hookrightarrow Aut(H_{k},\langle\,,\,\rangle) acting on the last kk components.

  2. 2)

    The reflection R123:(Hk,⟨,⟩)→(Hk,⟨,⟩)R_{123}:(H_{k},\langle\,,\,\rangle)\rightarrow(H_{k},\langle\,,\,\rangle) defined by R123​(η)=η+⟨η,r123⟩​r123R_{123}(\eta)=\eta+\langle\eta,r_{123}\rangle r_{123}, where r123=l−e1−e2−e3r_{123}=l-e_{1}-e_{2}-e_{3}.

The group C​rkCr_{k} is called the Cremona group.

It is easily seen that the reflections Ri​j​k​(η)=η+⟨η,ri​j​k⟩​ri​j​kR_{ijk}(\eta)=\eta+\langle\eta,r_{ijk}\rangle r_{ijk}, where ri​j​k=l−ei−ej−ekr_{ijk}=l-e_{i}-e_{j}-e_{k}, belong to C​rkCr_{k}. Let us mention one more useful transformation which we denote by S​RSR. The transformation S​RSR takes a vector v=(d,m1,…,mk)∈Hkv=(d;m_{1},\ldots,m_{k})\in H_{k} and sorts it. In other words S​R​(v)=(d,mτ⁡(1),…,mτ⁡(k))SR(v)=(d;m_{\tau(1)},\ldots,m_{\tau(k)}), where τ\tau is a permutation of {1,…,k}\{1,\ldots,k\} for which mτ⁡(1)≥…≥mτ⁡(k)m_{\tau(1)}\geq\ldots\geq m_{\tau(k)}. It is obvious that for every vector v∈Hkv\in H_{k} there exists σ∈C​rk\sigma\in Cr_{k} such that S​R​(v)=σ⁡(v)SR(v)=\sigma(v).

Given a simple rational surface obtained by blowing up Θ:V→ℂ​P2\Theta:V\rightarrow{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} of p1,…,pn∈ℂ​P2p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\in{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}, there is an isomorphism of lattices mΘ:(Pic(V),⋅)→(Hk,⟨,⟩)m_{\Theta}:(\mbox{Pic}(V),\,\cdot\,)\rightarrow(H_{k},\langle\,,\,\rangle), where ⋅\cdot stands for the intersection form on Pic​(V)\mbox{Pic}(V). The isomorphism mΘm_{\Theta} sends LVL^{V} to ll and EiVE^{V}_{i} to eie_{i}.

To deduce that C​rkCr_{k} acts on the set of ample (resp. nef) vectors we need the following lemma which essentially appears in [Do-Or].

Lemma 4.1.A.

Let VV be a simple rational surface obtained by blowing-up Θ:V→ℂ​P2\Theta:V\rightarrow{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} points p1,…,pn∈ℂ​P2p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\in{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} in general position. Then for every σ∈C​rk\sigma\in Cr_{k} there exists a simple rational surface VσV_{\sigma} obtained by blowing-up Θσ:Vσ→ℂ​P2\Theta_{\sigma}:V_{\sigma}\rightarrow{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} points q1,…​qkq_{1},\ldots q_{k} in general position and a biholomorphism fσ:Vσ→Vf_{\sigma}:V_{\sigma}\rightarrow V making the following diagram commutative:

Pic​(V)→fσ∗Pic​(Vσ)mΘ↓mΘσ↓Hk→σHk\begin{CD}\mbox{Pic}(V)@>{f^{*}_{\sigma}}>{}>\mbox{Pic}(V_{\sigma})\\ @V{m_{\Theta}}V{}V@V{m_{\Theta_{\sigma}}}V{}V\\ H_{k}@>{\sigma}>{}>H_{k}\end{CD}

Combining this with Lemma 3.1.A we immediately obtain the following

Lemma 4.1.B.

When k≥3k\geq 3 the group C​rkCr_{k} acts on the set of ample (resp. nef) vectors viewed as a subset of HkH_{k}.

Remark. From Lemma 3.1.A it follows that there exists (at least) one simple rational surface SS, obtained by blowing-up kk distinct points in ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}, Θ:S~→ℂ​P2\Theta:{\widetilde{S}}\rightarrow{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} such that ℒ∈Pic​(S){\cal{L}}\in\mbox{Pic}(S) is ample (resp. nef) iff mΘ​(ℒ)m_{\Theta}({\cal{L}}) is ample (resp. nef). Hence, the set of ample (resp. nef) vectors is closed under addition and multiplication by positive (resp. non-negative) integers. Henceforth we shall denote by 𝒦k⊂Hk⊗ℝ{\cal{K}}_{k}\subset H_{k}\otimes{\mathbb{R}} (resp. 𝒦¯k\overline{{\cal{K}}}_{k}) the cone generated by all ample (resp. nef) vectors.

4.2. An algorithmic procedure for detecting ample classes

Given two vectors v1=(d,m1,…,mn)∈Hnv_{1}=(d;m_{1},\ldots,m_{n})\in H_{n} and v2=(δ,α1,…,αk)∈Hkv_{2}=(\delta;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k})\in H_{k} with δ=mi\delta=m_{i} for some 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, define a new vector v1#iv2∈Hn+k−1v_{1}{\#_{{}_{i}}}v_{2}\in H_{n+k-1} by setting

v1#iv2=(d;m1,…,mi−1,α1,…,αk,mi+1,…,mn).v_{1}{\#_{{}_{i}}}v_{2}=(d;m_{1},\ldots,m_{i-1},\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k},m_{i+1},\ldots,m_{n}).

Theorem 2.A asserts that if v1v_{1} is ample (resp. nef) and v2v_{2} is nef, then v1#iv2v_{1}{\#_{{}_{i}}}v_{2} is ample (resp. nef).

Given a vector v0∈HNv_{0}\in H_{N} the ampleness of which we want to prove we try to find a decomposition v0=v1#i1u1v_{0}=v_{1}\#_{{}_{i_{1}}}u_{1} where u1∈Hk1u_{1}\in H_{k_{1}} is known to be nef and v1∈Hn1,(k1+n1−1=N)v_{1}\in H_{n_{1}},\,\,(k_{1}+n_{1}-1=N). If v1v_{1} turns to be ample then we are done in view of Theorem 2.A. To check the ampleness of v1v_{1} we first ”simplify” it by applying to it Cremona transformations. For example, we may try, using Cremona transformations to reduce the degree of v1v_{1} (by the degree of v=(d,μ1,…,μk)v=(d;\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{k}) we mean deg⁡v=d\deg\,v=d). Let v1′v_{1}^{\prime} be a simpler vector in the same orbit of v1v_{1} under the action of C​rn1Cr_{n_{1}} (e.g. v1′v_{1}^{\prime} having minimal degree in the orbit, or having some other convenient feature). By Lemma 4.1.B v1v_{1} is ample iff v1′v_{1}^{\prime} is. Now we apply the whole process to v1′v_{1}^{\prime} and so on. In this way we obtain a sequence of vectors v1,u1,v1′,…,vr,ur,vr′v_{1},u_{1},v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{r},u_{r},v_{r}^{\prime} where vj′v_{j}^{\prime} is a Cremona simplification of vj∈Hnjv_{j}\in H_{n_{j}}, uj∈Hkju_{j}\in H_{k_{j}} is a nef vector and vj′=vj+1#ij+1uj+1v_{j}^{\prime}=v_{j+1}\#_{{}_{i_{j+1}}}u_{j+1} for some ij+1i_{j+1}.

Note that at each stage the number of points decreases, namely nj+1<njn_{j+1}<n_{j} provided that kj>1k_{j}>1. The process ends successfully as soon as we are able to prove that vrv_{r} is ample for some rr. We remark that if one of the vjv_{j} turns out not to be ample then process fails to give any information because the converse of Theorem 2.A is not true. However, we may attempt to find other decomposition sequences v1,u1,v1′,…,vr,ur,vr′v_{1},u_{1},v_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{r},u_{r},v_{r}^{\prime} (see Section 6).

The same procedure can be applied for proving nefness of a vector v0v_{0} by requiring that vrv_{r} is nef instead of ample. In the next subsection we shall apply this process in order to prove Theorem 2.1.A and Corollary 2.1.B.

In order to make the preceding procedure applicable we must first endow ourselves with an initial large enough collection of ample and nef vectors which will play the role of the uju_{j}’s and of vrv_{r}. To simplify notations let us agree that (d,α1×r1,…​αk×rk)(d;\alpha_{1}^{\times r_{1}},\ldots\alpha_{k}^{\times r_{k}}) stands for

(d,α1,…,α1⏟r1 times,…​…,αk,…,αk⏟rk times)∈HN,(d;\underbrace{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{1}}_{\mbox{\tiny$r_{1}$ times}},\ldots\ldots,\underbrace{\alpha_{k},\ldots,\alpha_{k}}_{\mbox{\tiny$r_{k}$ times}})\in H_{N},

where N=∑j=1krjN=\sum_{j=1}^{k}r_{j}.

The next lemma provides a modest initial collection of ample and nef vectors which is sufficient for our purposes.

Lemma 4.2.A.

The following vectors are nef (resp. ample) on a very general rational surface:

  1. 1)

    (d;1×r)(d;1^{\times r}), where d2≥rd^{2}\geq r (resp. d2>rd^{2}>r).

  2. 2)

    (d,m1,m2,1×r)(d;m_{1},m_{2},1^{\times r}) where d≥m1+m2d\geq m_{1}+m_{2} and d2≥m12+m22+rd^{2}\geq m_{1}^{2}+m_{2}^{2}+r.

Remark. The “ample” case of statement 1 above has been proved by Xu in [Xu 2] and by Küchle in [Ku]. Below however, we present an alternative proof suggested by Ilya Tyomkin.

Proof.

Notice first that in view of Lemma 3.1.A it is enough to prove that the above vectors are nef (resp. ample) on a specific simple rational surface.

1) Consider first the case d2>rd^{2}>r. In [Nag] (consult also [Sh-Ty]) Nagata proved that if NN is a square, then for generic points p1,…,pN∈ℂ​P2p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}\in{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} and for every irreducible curve C⊂ℂ​P2C\subset{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} the following strict inequality holds:

(1) deg​(C)>∑j=1Nmultpj​(C)N.\mbox{deg}(C)>\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mbox{mult}_{p_{j}}(C)}{\sqrt{N}}.

Let VrV_{r} be the blow-up of ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} at rr generic points and denote by Θ:V~r→Vr\Theta:\widetilde{V}_{r}\rightarrow V_{r} the blow-up of VrV_{r} at d2−rd^{2}-r generic points. Thus V~r\widetilde{V}_{r} is the blow-up of ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} at N=d2N=d^{2} generic points and it follows from inequality (1) that the divisor D~=Θ∗​(d​LVr−∑j=1rEjVr)−∑j=r+1d2Ej\widetilde{D}=\Theta^{*}(dL^{V_{r}}-\sum_{j=1}^{r}E^{V_{r}}_{j})-\sum_{j=r+1}^{d^{2}}E_{j} intersects every curve positively. This immediately implies that D=d​LVr−∑j=1rEjVrD=dL^{V_{r}}-\sum_{j=1}^{r}E^{V_{r}}_{j} intersects any curve in VrV_{r} positively. As D⋅D>0D\cdot D>0 the statement follows from Nakai-Moishezon criterion (see [Ha 1]).

The proof for the nef case (d2≥rd^{2}\geq r) is much easier. Indeed, let C⊂ℂ​P2C\subset{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} be an irreducible curve of degree dd, and let p1,…,prp_{1},\ldots,p_{r} be distinct points on CC at which CC is smooth. Let VV be the blow-up of ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} at p1,…,prp_{1},\ldots,p_{r} and let DD be the proper transform of CC in VV, D∈|d​LV−∑j=1rEj|D\in|dL^{V}-\sum_{j=1}^{r}E_{j}|. As DD is an irreducible curve of non-negative self intersection the vector (d;1×r)(d;1^{\times r}) corresponding to the divisor class of DD is nef on VV.

2) Set D=d​L−m1​E1−m2​E2D=dL-m_{1}E_{1}-m_{2}E_{2}. Consider the linear system |D||D| on V2V_{2} – the blow-up of ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} at 2 points. As D=m1​(L−E1)+m2​(L−E2)+(d−m1−m2)​LD=m_{1}(L-E_{1})+m_{2}(L-E_{2})+(d-m_{1}-m_{2})L it is easy to see that |D||D| is not empty and has no base-points, hence by Bertini theorem there exists an irreducible (smooth) curve C∈|D|C\in|D|. Choose rr distinct points p1,…,pr∈C∖(E1∪E2)p_{1},\ldots,p_{r}\in C\setminus(E_{1}\cup E_{2}) and letV~\widetilde{V} be the blow-up of VV at p1,…,prp_{1},\ldots,p_{r}. Finally denote by C~\widetilde{C} be the proper transform of CC in V~\widetilde{V}.

We have C~∈|d​L−m1​E1−m2​E2−∑j=3r+2Ej|\widetilde{C}\in|dL-m_{1}E_{1}-m_{2}E_{2}-\sum_{j=3}^{r+2}E_{j}|. As C~\widetilde{C} is irreducible and C~⋅C~≥0\widetilde{C}\cdot\widetilde{C}\geq 0, the vector (d,m1,m2,1×r)(d;m_{1},m_{2},1^{\times r}) is nef.  

Remark. Note that the cones 𝒦n{\cal{K}}_{n} (resp. 𝒦¯n\overline{{\cal{K}}}_{n}) can be explicitly computed when n<9n<9 (see [Dmz], [F-M]), and so can be joined to the initial collection of ample and nef vectors to be applied in the framework of the process mentioned above.

5. A conjecture relating continued fractions and remainders of a line bundle

The goal of this section is to propose a conjecture concerning estimates on the values of the homogeneous remainders of 𝒪ℂ​P2​(1){\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1), defined in Section 2.1. It turns out that all the cases appearing in the statement of Theorem 2.1.A are particular cases of this conjecture.

Let us first recall some relevant facts from classical number theory. Given a square-free number NN, consider the following Diophantine equation in the unknowns d,md,m

d2−N​m2=1.d^{2}-Nm^{2}=1.

This equation had been attached-to the name Pell’s equation in the ancient literature and has been extensively studied by many mathematicians in the 17’th and 18’th centuries including Leonard Euler (see [Niv, Ir-Ro, VndP]). the classical result about the solutions of this equation is that all solutions come from continued fractions expansions of N\sqrt{N}. Let us write ⟨a0,a1,…,an⟩\langle a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\rangle for the continued fractions expansion

a0+1a1+1⋱+1an−1+1ana_{0}+\cfrac{1}{a_{1}+\cfrac{1}{\ddots+\cfrac{1}{a_{n-1}+\cfrac{1}{a_{n}}}}}

Similarly, we denote by ⟨a0,a1,…⟩\langle a_{0},a_{1},\ldots\rangle an infinite continued fractions expansion. It is not hard to see that the continued fractions expansion of N\sqrt{N} must be of the following special periodic form

N=⟨a0,a1,…,an−1,2​a0,a1,…,an−1,2​a0,…⟩,\sqrt{N}=\langle a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1},2a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1},2a_{0},\ldots\rangle,

hence we shall write from now on N=⟨a0,a1,…,an−1,2​a0¯⟩\sqrt{N}=\langle a_{0},\overline{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1},2a_{0}}\rangle where the bar denotes the periodic part. Moreover, it turns out that ai=an−ia_{i}=a_{n-i} for every 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1, (i.e. (a1,…,an−1)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1}) is a palindrome).

Define a rational number dm\frac{d}{m} as follows: if nn is even put

dm=⟨a0,a1,…,an−1⟩,\frac{d}{m}=\langle a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1}\rangle,

while for nn odd

dm=⟨a0,a1,…,an−1,2​a0,a1,…,an−1⟩.\frac{d}{m}=\langle a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1},2a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1}\rangle.

It is well known that (d,m)(d,m) provides the minimal solution of Pell’s equation, called the fundamental solution. Moreover, any other solution of Pell’s equation is obtained in a similar manner – by truncating the infinite continued fraction of N\sqrt{N} one term before the end of one of its periods. More precisely, (d,m)(d,m) solves Pell’s equation iff

dm=⟨a0,a1,…,an−1,2​a0¯×r,a1,…,an−1⟩,where r is odd if n is odd.\frac{d}{m}=\langle a_{0},\overline{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1},2a_{0}}^{\,\times r},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1}\rangle,\,\,\,\mbox{where $r$ is odd if $n$ is odd}.

This formula means that the periodic part a1,…​an−1,2​a0a_{1},\ldots a_{n-1},2a_{0} should be taken rr times and then once more without the last member 2​a02a_{0}. The number rr is allowed to be any non-negative integer in case nn is even, and rr must be odd if nn is odd.

Our conjecture is the following

Conjecture 5.A.

Let N>9N>9 be a square-free number and let dm\frac{d}{m} be the fundamental solution of the corresponding Pell’s equation. Then:
1) The vector (d;m×N)(d;m^{\times N}) is nef.
2) ℛN​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1))≤1d2{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1))\leq\frac{1}{d^{2}}.

Our conjecture is much weaker than Nagata’s, on the other hand it seems more accessible. Indeed, our methods provide a proof for the conjecture in the following cases:

1. Consider the case that N\sqrt{N} has a 2-periodic continued fractions expansion N=⟨a0,a1,2​a0¯⟩\sqrt{N}=\langle a_{0},\overline{a_{1},2a_{0}}\rangle. It is easy to see that this is the case iff a1|2​a0a_{1}|2a_{0} and N=a02+2​a0a1N=a_{0}^{2}+2\frac{a_{0}}{a_{1}}. The solution of Pell’s equation is d=10​a1+1,m=a1d=1_{0}a_{1}+1,\;m=a_{1}.

  1. A)

    Suppose that a1|a0a_{1}|a_{0}. Putting a=a1a=a_{1} and l=a0a1l=\frac{a_{0}}{a_{1}} we get N=a2​l2+2​lN=a^{2}l^{2}+2l, and so by Theorem 2.1.A our conjecture holds in this case.

  2. B)

    Suppose that a1∤a0a_{1}\nmid a_{0} and 2k​a0>a122^{k}a_{0}>a_{1}^{2}, where kk is the maximal integer for which 2k|a12^{k}|a_{1}. Since a1|2​a0a_{1}|2a_{0}, a1a_{1} must be even. Putting a=a12a=\frac{a_{1}}{2} and l=2​a0a1l=\frac{2a_{0}}{a_{1}} we obtain N=a2​l2+lN=a^{2}l^{2}+l and l>a2k−2l>\frac{a}{2^{k-2}}. By Theorem 2.1.A our conjecture holds.


2. Consider NN’s of the form N=a2​l2−2​lN=a^{2}l^{2}-2l. It is not hard to see that d=a2​l−1,m=ad=a^{2}l-1,m=a satisfy Pell’s equation d2−N​m2=1d^{2}-Nm^{2}=1. By Theorem 2.1.A we have ℛN​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1))≤1d2{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1))\leq\frac{1}{d^{2}}. Therefore, if (d′,m′)(d^{\prime},m^{\prime}) is the fundamental solution of Pell’s equation then ℛN​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1))≤1d2≤1d′2{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1))\leq\frac{1}{d^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{{d^{\prime}}^{2}}, and so the conjecture holds. Note that in this case the expansion of N\sqrt{N} will usually be longer than 2 (example: 14=⟨3,1,2,1,6¯⟩\sqrt{14}=\langle 3,\overline{1,2,1,6}\rangle).44 4 It is not hard to see that if N=a2​l2−2​lN=a^{2}l^{2}-2l then N\sqrt{N} has 2-periodic expansion with minus signs.

3. Let us mention two other examples which do not fall into the above categories.

  1. A)

    N=19N=19. In this case 19=⟨4,2,1,3,1,2,8¯⟩\sqrt{19}=\langle 4,\overline{2,1,3,1,2,8}\rangle. The fundamental solution is d=170,m=39d=170,m=39. Thus, our conjecture suggests that ℛ19​(𝒪ℂ​P2​(1))≤11702{\cal{R}}_{19}({\cal O}_{{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}}(1))\leq\frac{1}{{170}^{2}}.

  2. B)

    N=22N=22. In this case 22=⟨4,1,2,4,2,1,8¯⟩\sqrt{22}=\langle 4,\overline{1,2,4,2,1,8}\rangle. The fundamental solution is d=197,m=42d=197,m=42. Thus, our conjecture suggests that ℛ22≤11972{\cal{R}}_{22}\leq\frac{1}{{197}^{2}}.

Let us prove that the conjecture indeed holds in the cases 3.A and 3.B. We start with N=19N=19. By Lemma 4.2.A the vector u=39​(2,1×4)=(78;39×4)u=39(2;1^{\times 4})=(78;39^{\times 4}) is nef. We have

(170;39×19)=(((170;78×3,39×7)#3u)#2u)#1u.(170;39^{\times 19})=(\,(\,(170;78^{\times 3},39^{\times 7})\#_{{}_{3}}u)\#_{{}_{2}}u)\#_{{}_{1}}u.

  1. 1)

    Replace vv by R123​(v)R_{123}(v).

  2. 2)

Applying this process enough times we finally arrive to the vector (1;0×10)(1;0^{\times 10}) which is nef.

The case N=22N=22 is similar. Here we use the decomposition

(197;42×22)=((((197;84×4,42×6)#4u)#3u)#2u)#1u,(197;42^{\times 22})=(\,(\,(\,(197;84^{\times 4},42^{\times 6})\#_{{}_{4}}u)\#_{{}_{3}}u)\#_{{}_{2}}u)\#_{{}_{1}}u,

with u=42​(2,1×4)=(84;42×4).u=42(2;1^{\times 4})=(84;42^{\times 4}). Applying the preceding process successively to (197,84×4,42×6)(197;84^{\times 4},42^{\times 6}) we obtain again the vector (1;0×10)(1;0^{\times 10}) which is nef.

6. The limits of the algorithm

In its present version, the algorithm described in Section 4.2 has the disadvantage that it does not tell which decomposition vj′=vj+1​#​uj+1v^{\prime}_{j}=v_{j+1}\#u_{j+1} one should choose at each stage in order the whole process to end successfully. We would like to emphasize that this decision is sometimes crucial as the following example shows:
Let v0=(10;3×11)∈H11v_{0}=(10;3^{\times 11})\in H_{11}. if one tries to decompose v0v_{0} as v0=(10,3×2,9)​#​(9,3×9)v_{0}=(10;3^{\times 2},9)\#(9;3^{\times 9}) the process will fail to give any information on v0v_{0}. The reason is that although (9;3×9)(9;3^{\times 9}) is nef (10,3×2,9)(10;3^{\times 2},9) is not, and so we cannot apply the gluing theorem. However, the decomposition v0=(10,3×7,6)​#​(6,34)v_{0}=(10;3^{\times 7},6)\#(6;3^{4}) will eventually lead to a successful ending of the algorithm, thus proving that v0v_{0} is nef. It would be useful of course to find a rule for choosing the “optimal” decomposition at each stage.

Finally, let us mention one simple example for which it seems that the algorithm fails to give information always. Consider the vector v0=(19,6×10)v_{0}=(19,6^{\times 10}) which by Nagata’s conjecture should be ample. However, it seems that the vector v0v_{0} is indecomposable in the sense that it is impossible to find even nef vectors v1∈Hn1,u1∈Hk1v_{1}\in H_{n_{1}},u_{1}\in H_{k_{1}} with n1,k1<10n_{1},k_{1}<10, such that v0′=v1​#​v2v_{0}^{\prime}=v_{1}\#v_{2} lies in the same orbit as v0v_{0} under the Cremona action. It would be interesting to find the precise conditions for an ample (resp. nef) vector vv to be indecomposable.

7. Symplectic interpretations

The purpose of this section is to explain the intuition which give rise to the gluing Theorem 2.B. Interestingly enough this comes from symplectic geometry.

Symplectic geometry is the branch of geometry dealing with the structure of symplectic manifolds which are by definition pairs, (M,Ω)(M,\Omega), consisting of a smooth manifold MM and a non-degenerated closed differential 2-form Ω\Omega. The reader is referred to [A-G] and [M-S] for the foundations.

Due to developments in this field of research in the last decade, many analogies has been discovered between symplectic and complex manifolds. These become especially striking in dimension 4, where symplectic 4-manifolds play the role of complex surfaces. In several cases it turned out that algebro-geometric considerations, remain true when properly translated into the symplectic category, and so gave rise to new theorems in the symplectic framework. This principle is reflected very well in the classification of rational and ruled symplectic manifolds of Lalonde and McDuff, in the symplectic packing theorems of McDuff and Polterovich, in Ruan’s symplectization of the extremal rays theory etc.

In this paper we have, in some sense, reversed this direction of reasoning. Our main theorem is in fact an algebro-geometric translation of a very simple symplectic fact arising from the theory of symplectic packing. We refer the reader to [M-P] for an excellent exposition on the symplectic packing problem.

Recall from [M-P] that a symplectic packing of (M,Ω)(M,\Omega) by NN balls of radii λ1,…,λN\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{N} is a symplectic embedding

φ=∐j=1Nφj:∐j=1NB⁡(λj)→(M,Ω),\varphi=\coprod_{j=1}^{N}\varphi_{j}:\coprod_{j=1}^{N}B(\lambda_{j})\rightarrow(M,\Omega),

where B⁡(λj)B(\lambda_{j}) stands for the standard Euclidean closed ball of radius λj\lambda_{j} of the same dimension as MM, endowed with its standard symplectic structure ωs​t​d=d​x1∧d​y1+…+d​xn∧d​yn\omega_{std}=dx_{1}\wedge dy_{1}+\ldots+dx_{n}\wedge dy_{n}.

It was discovered by McDuff that every symplectic packing gives rise to a symplectic form Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} on the blow-up Θ:M~→M\Theta:{\widetilde{M}}\rightarrow M of MM at the points p1=φ1​(0),…​pN=φN​(0)p_{1}=\varphi_{1}(0),\ldots p_{N}=\varphi_{N}(0). This form lies in the cohomology class

(1) [Ω~]=[Θ∗​Ω]−π​∑j=1Nλj2​ej,[\widetilde{\Omega}]=[\Theta^{*}\Omega]-\pi\sum_{j=1}^{N}\lambda_{j}^{2}e_{j},

where eje_{j} denotes the Poincaré dual to the homology class of the exceptional divisor EjE_{j} of the blow-up. This procedure is called symplectic blowing-up.

Conversely, given a symplectic form Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} on M~{\widetilde{M}} which is non-degenerated on the exceptional divisors EjE_{j} and with cohomology class as in (1) above, one can perform symplectic blowing-down at the exceptional divisors and obtain a symplectic form Ω\Omega on MM and a symplectic packing φ=∐j=1Nφj:∐j=1NB⁡(λj)→(M,Ω)\varphi=\coprod_{j=1}^{N}\varphi_{j}:\coprod_{j=1}^{N}B(\lambda_{j})\rightarrow(M,\Omega).

Consider the symplectic manifold (ℂ​P2,σ)({\mathbb{C}}P^{2},\sigma) where σ\sigma is the Fubini-Studi Kähler form normalized such that the area of a projective line is π\pi. Its cohomology class is π​l\pi l, where l∈H2​(ℂ​P2,ℤ)l\in H^{2}({{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}},{\mathbb{Z}}) is the standard positive generator.

Call a vector of positive numbers (d,m1,…,mk)(d;m_{1},\ldots,m_{k}) symplectic if the cohomology class

d​ΘV∗​l−∑j=1kmj​ejd\Theta_{V}^{*}l-\sum_{j=1}^{k}m_{j}e_{j}

can be represented by a symplectic form ω~\widetilde{\omega} on some blow-up ΘV:V→ℂ​P2\Theta_{V}:V\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}P^{2} of ℂ​P2{\mathbb{C}}P^{2} at some kk distinct points, in such a way that ω~\widetilde{\omega} is non-degenerated on the exceptional divisors.

Now, let MM be a complex surface and Θp:M~p→M\Theta_{p}:{\widetilde{M}}_{p}\rightarrow M its blow-up at the point p∈Mp\in M with exceptional divisor EE. Denote by ee the Poincaré dual to the homology class of EE.

Proposition 7.A.

Let a∈H2​(M)a\in H^{2}(M) and suppose that there exists a positive number mm such that the cohomology class Θp∗​a−m​e∈H2​(M~p)\Theta_{p}^{*}a-me\in H^{2}({\widetilde{M}}_{p}) can be represented by a symplectic form whose restriction to EE is non-degenerated.55 5 This means that EE is a symplectic submanifold with respect to this form. Then, for every symplectic vector (m,α1,…,αk)(m;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}), the cohomology class Θ∗​a−∑j=1kαj​ej\Theta^{*}a-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}e_{j} on the blow-up Θ:M~→M\Theta:{\widetilde{M}}\rightarrow M at some kk points can be represented by a symplectic form.

The proof is based on the following very simple observation. If Θp∗​a−m​e\Theta_{p}^{*}a-me has a symplectic representative Ω~\widetilde{\Omega}, then by symplectic blowing down one obtains a symplectic form Ω\Omega on MM and an embedding φ\varphi of a standard 4-dimensional ball of radius mπ\sqrt{\frac{m}{\pi}} into (M,Ω)(M,\Omega). The same argument with slight modifications, applied to the vector (m,α1,…,αk)(m;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}), implies that the standard ball of radius mπ\sqrt{\frac{m}{\pi}} admits a symplectic packing, say ϕ\phi, by kk balls of radii α1π,…,αkπ\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\pi}},\ldots,\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{k}}{\pi}}. Composing these two embeddings we conclude that (M,Ω)(M,\Omega) admits a symplectic packing φ∘ϕ\varphi\circ\phi of kk balls of radii α1π,…,αkπ\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\pi}},\ldots,\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{k}}{\pi}}. The proposition follows now from symplectic blowing-up. For completeness, here are the precise arguments of the proof.

Proof.

Let Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} be a symplectic form on M~p{\widetilde{M}}_{p} lying in the cohomology class Θp∗​a−m​e\Theta_{p}^{*}a-me and suppose that the restriction of Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} to EE is non-degenerated. Applying symplectic blowing-down to Ω~\widetilde{\Omega} we obtain a symplectic form Ω\Omega on MM lying in the cohomology class aa and a symplectic embedding φ:B⁡(mπ)→(M,Ω)\varphi:B(\sqrt{\frac{m}{\pi}})\rightarrow(M,\Omega).

Let ω~\widetilde{\omega} be a symplectic form on the blow-up π:V→ℂ​P2\pi:V\rightarrow{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} of ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} lying in the cohomology class m​ΘV∗​l−∑j=1kαj​ejm\Theta_{V}^{*}l-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}e_{j} and whose restriction to the exceptional divisors EjE_{j} is non-degenerated. Blowing-down symplectically we obtain a symplectic form ω\omega on ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} lying in the cohomology class m​lml and a symplectic packing ψ:∐j=1kB⁡(αjπ)→(ℂ​P2,ω)\psi:\coprod_{j=1}^{k}B(\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{j}}{\pi}})\rightarrow({{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}},\omega). Since any two cohomologous symplectic forms on ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} are symplectomorphic we may assume that ω=mπ​σ\omega=\frac{m}{\pi}\sigma. It can be proved by the methods of [M-P] that there exists a symplectic submanifold (with respect to ω\omega) L⊂ML\subset M, homologous to a projective line, which is disjoint from Image​ψ\mbox{Image}\;\psi. It is well known that (ℂ​P2∖L,mπ​σ)≈B⁡(mπ)({{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}}\setminus L,\frac{m}{\pi}\sigma)\approx B(\sqrt{\frac{m}{\pi}}). We thus obtain a symplectic packing ϕ:∐j=1kB⁡(αjπ)→B⁡(mπ)\phi:\coprod_{j=1}^{k}B(\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{j}}{\pi}})\rightarrow B(\sqrt{\frac{m}{\pi}}).

The composition φ∘ϕ\varphi\circ\phi is a symplectic packing of (M,Ω)(M,\Omega) by kk balls of radii α1π,…,αkπ\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\pi}},\ldots,\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{k}}{\pi}}. Blowing-up symplectically with respect to this embedding yields a symplectic form on the blow-up Θ:M~→M\Theta:{\widetilde{M}}\rightarrow M of MM at kk points, which lies in the cohomology class Θ∗​a−∑j=1kαj​ej\Theta^{*}a-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}e_{j}.  

Let us try to translate Proposition 7.A to the language of algebraic geometry. Keeping in mind that in the symplectic category the role of Kähler forms is played by symplectic forms and the role of complex submanifolds by symplectic submanifolds, the Kählerian translation should read: “If the cohomology class Θp∗​a−m​e\Theta_{p}^{*}a-me has a Kähler representative than for every Kähler vector (m,α1,…,αk)(m;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}) the cohomology class Θ∗​a−∑j=1kαj​ej\Theta^{*}a-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}e_{j} has a Kähler representative too”.
Here, we call a vector (m,α1,…,αk)(m;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}) Kähler if the cohomology class

m​ΘV∗​l−∑j=1kαj​ejm\Theta_{V}^{*}l-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}e_{j}

can be represented by a Kähler form ω~\widetilde{\omega} on some simple rational surface ΘV:V→ℂ​P2\Theta_{V}:V\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}P^{2} obtained by blowing-up ℂ​P2{\mathbb{C}}P^{2} at some kk distinct points.

Due to Lefschetz theorem on (1,1)(1,1) classes and Kodaira’s embedding theorem it follows that on a complex manifold there is a bijection – via Poincaré duality – between the set of homology classes of ample ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-divisors and the set of rational cohomology classes which can be represented by Kähler forms. Poincaré dualizing the “Kählerian translation” we are naturally led to the following: “Let DD be a divisor on MM such that Θp∗​D−m​E\Theta_{p}^{*}D-mE is ample. Then for every ample vector (m,α1,…,αk)(m;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}) the divisor Θ∗​D−∑j=1kαj​Ej\Theta^{*}D-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}E_{j} is ample too”. This is precisely the contents of Theorem 2.B for the case that MM is a simple rational surface. The technical machinery which made the whole translation rigorous is Shustin’s curve gluing technique which we used in Section 3.

We would like to emphasize that the same “symplectic reasoning” suggests that if we replace the surface SS in the statement of Theorem 2.B by any projective surface, the Theorem should remain true. Similar symplectic arguments suggest that an appropriate version of Theorem 2.B should hold also for higher dimensions than 2. It would be of course interesting to know whether Theorem 2.B continues to hold for smooth algebraic surfaces over an arbitrary algebraically closed field. We leave these discussions to another opportunity.

7.1. Symplectic meaning of the remainders ℛN​(ℒ){\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal{L}})

In section 2.1 we have defined the homogeneous remainders ℛN​(ℒ){\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal{L}}) of an ample line bundle ℒ{\cal{L}} over a surface. The definition naturally extends to nn-dimensional smooth varieties XX in the following obvious way. Given p1,…,pN∈Xp_{1},\ldots,p_{N}\in X, set

ℛ(ℒ,p1,…,pN)=1ℒninf0≤ϵ∈ℝ{ℒϵn|ℒϵ=π∗ℒ−ϵ∑j=1NEjis nef},{\cal{R}}({\cal{L}},p_{1},\ldots,p_{N})=\frac{1}{{\cal{L}}^{n}}\inf_{0\leq\epsilon\in{\mathbb{R}}}\left\{{\cal{L}}_{\epsilon}^{n}\bigg|{\cal{L}}_{\epsilon}=\pi^{*}{\cal{L}}-\epsilon\sum_{j=1}^{N}E_{j}\quad\mbox{is nef}\right\},

where π:X~→X\pi:{\widetilde{X}}\rightarrow X is the blow-up of XX at the points p1,…,pNp_{1},\ldots,p_{N} with exceptional divisors Ei=π−1​(pi)E_{i}=\pi^{-1}(p_{i}). To get a more global invariant, define

ℛN(ℒ)=inf{ℛ(ℒ,p1,…pN)∣p1,…pN∈Xare distinct points}.{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal{L}})=\inf\left\{{\cal{R}}({\cal{L}},p_{1},\ldots p_{N})\mid p_{1},\ldots p_{N}\in X\quad\mbox{are distinct points}\right\}.

Let us explain now the symplectic meaning of these constants. Let (M,Ω)(M,\Omega) be a symplectic manifold. Following McDuff and Polterovich define the following quantity

vN​(M,Ω)=supφ,λVol​(Image ​φ)Vol​(M,Ω),v_{N}(M,\Omega)=\sup_{\varphi,\,\lambda}\frac{\mbox{Vol}(\mbox{Image\, }\varphi)}{\mbox{Vol}(M,\Omega)},

where (φ,λ)(\varphi,\lambda) passes over all the possible symplectic packings φ\varphi of (M,Ω)(M,\Omega) with NN equal balls of varying radius λ\lambda. The volume of the manifolds is defined to be Vol​(M,Ω)=∫M1n!​Ω∧n\mbox{Vol}(M,\Omega)=\int_{M}\frac{1}{n!}\Omega^{\wedge n}.

The constants vN​(M,Ω)v_{N}(M,\Omega) admit values between 00 and 11 and measure the maximal part of the volume of (M,Ω)(M,\Omega) which can be filled by symplectic packing with NN equal balls. When vN=1v_{N}=1 we say that there exists a full packing of (M,Ω)(M,\Omega) by NN equal balls, while in the case vN<1v_{N}<1 we say that there exists a packing obstruction.

In view of the preceding discussion it is easy to see that the homogeneous remainders ℛN​(ℒ){\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal{L}}) of an ample line bundle over a complex manifold MM, play the algebro-geometric role of the quantity 1−vN​(M,Ω)1-v_{N}(M,\Omega), where Ω\Omega is a Kähler form representing the first Chern class of ℒ,c1​(ℒ){\cal{L}},\;c_{1}({\cal{L}}). In fact, it is not hard to prove that the following inequality holds

(2) 1−vN​(M,Ω)≤ℛN​(ℒ).1-v_{N}(M,\Omega)\leq{\cal{R}}_{N}({\cal{L}}).

Note that there are cases in which one always has equality in (2). For example, it follows from the work of McDuff and Polterovich (see [M-P]) that this is the case for ℂ​P2{{\mathbb{C}}P^{2}} when N<9N<9. The point is that the symplectic cone and the Kähler cone of del Pezzo surfaces coincide. Note that in (real) dimension 4, more is known about the constants vNv_{N} than about ℛN{\cal{R}}_{N} (see [Bi]). It would be interesting to know whether there exist cases in which a strict inequality occurs in (2).

Let us conclude by pointing out another interesting approach to bounding Seshadri constants via symplectic packing, due to Lazarsfeld (see [Laz]). The idea is that given a Kähler form Ω\Omega on a complex manifold and a symplectic packing φ\varphi which is also holomorphic, the symplectic blow-up of Ω\Omega associated to φ\varphi will be Kähler. This situation happens when the associated Kähler metric on the image of φ\varphi is flat. Applying this to the case of a principally polarized abelian variety, Lazarsfeld obtains non-trivial estimates on Seshadri constatnts of the corresponding ample divisor.
